items.subtype: Modifier placement: preposition + gerund opener (Despite consisting of ...), mid-sentence blank; the right subject is “Bašić’s Sea Organ,” a possessive phrase built on the architect named first
items.passage: In 2005, Croatian architect Nikola Bašić turned stone steps on the Zadar waterfront into a musical instrument, the Sea Organ. Despite consisting of little more than stone slabs and plastic pipes, ______ whenever incoming waves force air through the partially submerged pipes beneath the steps and out through openings in the promenade above.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: an ever-changing series of low, breathy chords is sounded by Bašić’s Sea Organ
it is Bašić’s Sea Organ that sounds an ever-changing series of low, breathy chords
Bašić’s Sea Organ sounds an ever-changing series of low, breathy chords
the music of Bašić’s Sea Organ is an ever-changing series of low, breathy chords
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Despite consisting of little more than stone slabs and plastic pipes,” describes a physical object: the instrument. Choice C places “Bašić’s Sea Organ” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the Sea Organ, made of stone and pipes, sounds the chords. The possessive “Bašić’s” only tells whose instrument it is; the subject is “Sea Organ.”

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the chords, passive clause with the same facts
A.why_wrong: “An ever-changing series of low, breathy chords” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the chords consist of little more than stone slabs and plastic pipes.

B.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has nothing it can logically describe; the Sea Organ appears only later, inside the clause.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the music of Bašić’s Sea Organ,” so the sentence illogically says that the music consists of stone slabs and plastic pipes.

items.notes: Subject: the Sea Organ in Zadar, Croatia, by architect Nikola Bašić (2005), white stone steps whose buried pipes are sounded by waves (arts, architecture and sound). Real work; facts kept general (opened 2005, steps on the Zadar waterfront, pipes under the steps, sound through openings in the upper steps). Band 7 as 37e5c794: a property opener (made of simple materials, a different gerund from the model’s “Despite being”) and options that all keep the same facts; the key starts with a possessive on the obvious noun (the architect, subject of the first sentence), which a student may wrongly reject as an agent buried in a possessive, while every option keeps the same facts and the same noun phrase “Bašić’s Sea Organ”: A is the passive with the chords first, B the cleft, D the nominalisation “the music of”. Recipes W, E, N, as 37e5c794 (E, W, P). Reviewer rebuilt A (it was “Bašić designed the steps to sound ...”, a change of claim that a student could reject on sense alone). 21 words of the run follow the blank. Each option tested in full: only C gives the opener a subject it can describe.
band7_moves: property opener (band-7 file, section 5, R3 rows): “Despite consisting of little more than stone slabs and plastic pipes” fits only the instrument
right subject is a possessive noun phrase built on the obvious noun (section 3, move 7): “Bašić’s Sea Organ,” with the architect as the subject of the first sentence
all three foils keep every fact and the key’s noun phrase: A passive with the chords as subject (W), B the cleft “it is ... that” (E), D “the music of” (N)
21 run words after the blank, so the sentence still reads as complete with every option

band7.why: After the rebuild of A it follows 37e5c794: a property opener (made of simple materials), all four options carry the same facts and the noun phrase “Bašić’s Sea Organ”, foils E, W and N, and 21 run words after the blank. Borderline: the key is the plain thing, not a property phrase (“the Y of X”), the pattern 3 of 5 band-7 R3 officials use.

fixes: rebuilt A as the same claim with the wrong subject first (passive, chords as subject) so every option keeps the same facts, as 37e5c794
trimmed the first sentence (“a flight of white” cut)

items.subtype: Modifier placement: -ing participial opener (Radiating outward ... and incised ...), passage-final blank; the channels are the right subject
items.passage: Each spring near the Martian south pole, sunlight penetrates a translucent slab of carbon dioxide ice and warms the soil underneath, causing the slab’s underside to sublimate into gas. Radiating outward like a spider’s legs and incised into the underlying soil, ______
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the channels known as araneiforms are thought to be carved by this gas as it escapes through cracks in the ice.
planetary scientists’ view is that this gas carves the channels known as araneiforms as it escapes through cracks in the ice.
this gas is thought to carve the channels known as araneiforms as it escapes through cracks in the ice.
the carving of the channels known as araneiforms is thought to be done by this gas as it escapes through cracks in the ice.
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “Radiating outward like a spider’s legs and incised into the underlying soil,” describes features cut into the Martian surface. Choice A places “the channels known as araneiforms” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the channels radiate outward and are incised into the soil.

B.why_wrong: The subject is “planetary scientists’ view,” so the sentence illogically says that a view radiates outward like a spider’s legs and is incised into the soil.

C.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the gas
C.why_wrong: “This gas” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that the gas is incised into the underlying soil.

D.why_wrong: The subject is “the carving of the channels,” so the sentence illogically says that an act of carving radiates outward and is incised into the soil.

items.notes: Subject: araneiforms, the spider-like channel networks near the south pole of Mars, explained by carbon dioxide gas that builds up under translucent seasonal ice and escapes through cracks (science, planetary science). Real phenomenon; facts kept general (spring sunlight through translucent CO2 ice warms the soil, ice turns to gas from below, escaping gas scours channels). No researchers named. Band 6 as 9df6da04 and dab8b8ee: -ing opener, passage-final blank, full-clause options that keep the same facts. Recipes P, W, N. The opener has two parts so that “incised into the underlying soil” rules out the gas (C) on meaning, not on grammar.

band7.why: Planned band 6. As 9df6da04 and dab8b8ee: options keep the same facts, the key is a passive with the right subject first, and the foils are the possessive view, the gas (the obvious noun from the first sentence) and a nominalisation.

fixes: trimmed “dark”

items.subtype: Modifier placement: noun-phrase appositive opener (A catalog of offenses ...), mid-sentence blank; the law code is the right subject
items.passage: The earliest known legal code survives only on fragmentary clay tablets from ancient Sumer. A catalog of offenses and their corresponding penalties, many of them fines payable in silver, ______ to around 2100 BCE, when the city of Ur controlled much of southern Mesopotamia.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Ur-Nammu, a king of the city of Ur, issued a code that dates
it is the Code of Ur-Nammu, named for a king of Ur, that dates
the drafting of the Code of Ur-Nammu, named for a king of Ur, dates
the Code of Ur-Nammu, named for a king of Ur, dates
items.explanation: The opening phrase, “A catalog of offenses and their corresponding penalties, many of them fines payable in silver,” describes a set of laws. Choice D places “the Code of Ur-Nammu” right after the phrase, so the sentence clearly says that the code is the catalog of offenses and penalties.

A.recipe: wrong noun as subject (W): the king
A.why_wrong: “Ur-Nammu, a king of the city of Ur,” follows the phrase, so the sentence illogically says that a king is a catalog of offenses and penalties.

B.why_wrong: The word “it” follows the phrase, so the phrase has nothing it can logically describe; the code appears only later, inside the clause.

C.why_wrong: The subject is “the drafting of the Code of Ur-Nammu,” so the sentence illogically says that an act of drafting is a catalog of offenses and penalties.

items.notes: Subject: the Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest known surviving law code, written in Sumerian around 2100 BCE, known from tablet fragments (the first identified copy from Nippur), with fines in silver for many injuries (history, law). Real; facts kept general (attributed to King Ur-Nammu, founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, which ruled much of southern Mesopotamia; about 2100 BCE). Hammurabi is not named: an official Transitions item is about him and his code. Band 6 as 5b8f9cf2: a long appositive opener, mid-sentence blank, the key a plain noun phrase plus a nonrestrictive participial phrase. Recipes W, E, N. No option uses a possessive on “Ur-Nammu,” since “Ur-Nammu’s code” would also be a correct subject.

band7.why: R3_appositive has no band-7 official item, so a strong band 6: a two-part appositive opener and foils W (the king), E and N that keep every fact.

items.subtype: Subject-verb agreement, be-family: singular head (system) behind a relative clause and a dash-enclosed appositive full of plurals with its own verb (allowed)
items.passage: After her husband’s death in 1848, Martha Coston discovered his preliminary sketches for nighttime signal flares. The signaling system she developed from those sketches—flares burning in combinations of red, white, and green that allowed sailors to transmit coded messages—______ purchased by the US Navy and used widely during the Civil War.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the second sentence is the singular noun “system”; everything between it and the blank, including the dash-enclosed description of the flares, only describes that system. The singular verb “was” agrees with “system” and fits the past events the sentence reports.

A.why_wrong: The plural verb “were” agrees with the nearby plurals “flares” or “messages,” not with the singular subject “system.”

C.why_wrong: The plural verb “are” does not agree with the singular subject “system.”

D.why_wrong: The plural verb “have been” does not agree with the singular subject “system.”

items.notes: Subject: Martha Coston, who developed her late husband Benjamin Franklin Coston’s rough notes into the Coston night-signal flares (red, white and green), patented in 1859, bought by the US Navy and used in the Civil War (history, invention). Real; facts kept general. Band 6 as ea0aa676: 21 words between the head and the blank, with five plural nouns and a past verb (“allowed”) inside the dash-enclosed appositive, so “were” sounds right twice. Options: wrong number in three tenses.

band7.why: Planned band 6, as ea0aa676: about 21 words and five plurals between the singular head and the blank, with a past verb (“allowed”) inside the dash-enclosed appositive.

fixes: “eventually” cut; notes and subtype named the intervener verb “let”, the passage has “allowed”

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: purpose infinitive after a compound predicate (compiled and then compared ...), against -ing, past and and + -ing
items.passage: Luminous flashes in the sky before or during earthquakes have been reported for centuries, but such fleeting events are difficult to study systematically. In 2014, four researchers compiled and then compared accounts of dozens of earthquakes accompanied by these lights ______ the geological settings in which the lights most often appear.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence already has its subject and its verbs: “four researchers compiled and then compared accounts.” The blank begins a phrase explaining why the researchers did this. The to-infinitive “to identify” correctly expresses that purpose.

B.recipe: wrong nonfinite: -ing participle with no comma
B.why_wrong: Without a comma, “identifying” attaches to the nearest noun, so the sentence illogically suggests that the lights were identifying the geological settings.

C.recipe: finite where a nonfinite phrase is needed
C.why_wrong: Without a conjunction such as “and,” the past tense verb “identified” cannot be added to the researchers’ actions in this way.

D.why_wrong: Joined by “and” to the past tense verbs “compiled” and “compared,” the form “identifying” is not parallel with them, and read as a participle it has no main clause to attach to.

items.notes: Subject: earthquake lights and a 2014 analysis of reported cases in the Americas and Europe, which found that most occurred near rift zones (science, geophysics). Real study (four authors: Thériault, St-Laurent, Freund, Derr); not named here, facts kept general (2014, dozens of earthquakes, accounts compared to find the settings). Band 6 by plan (R2_to_inf has no band-7 official item), built as 512f0ac9: purpose infinitive after a compound predicate, options to + base, -ing, past, and + -ing. The noun right before the blank (“lights”) cannot identify anything, so “identifying” fails on meaning as well as structure, as “forging” does in the model.

band7.why: R2_to_inf has no band-7 official item, so a strong band 6 built as 512f0ac9 (purpose infinitive after a compound predicate; -ing, past and and + -ing foils).

fixes: “four geophysicists” softened to “four researchers” (the real authors include a geologist and a physicist)
tested all four options in the full sentence: exactly one is grammatical

items.subtype: Plural vs possessive nouns: individual possession of two mass nouns (saffron’s and turmeric’s), the cue that each has its own pigment after the blank
items.passage: Saffron and turmeric have long been used to dye textiles and foods a similar golden yellow, and the far cheaper turmeric is sometimes sold in markets as counterfeit saffron. Chemically, however, ______ pigments are unrelated, with each spice’s coloration produced by a separate family of compounds: water-soluble carotenoids called crocins in saffron and fat-soluble polyphenols called curcuminoids in turmeric.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Each spice has its own pigments, as the phrase “with each spice’s coloration produced by a separate family of compounds” makes clear. To show that each of two nouns possesses something separately, both nouns take the possessive. The singular possessives “saffron’s and turmeric’s” correctly indicate that the pigments belong to each spice individually.

A.recipe: plural for possessive in both slots
A.why_wrong: The context requires the possessives “saffron’s” and “turmeric’s,” not the plurals “saffrons” and “turmerics.”

B.recipe: plural for possessive in the first slot
B.why_wrong: The context requires the singular possessive “saffron’s,” not the plural “saffrons.”

C.recipe: joint possession where each owns separately
C.why_wrong: With only “turmeric’s” marked, the phrase suggests that the two spices share a single set of colors, whereas the text says that each spice’s coloration is produced by a separate family of compounds.

items.notes: Subject: why saffron and turmeric are both yellow: crocins (water-soluble carotenoids) in saffron and curcuminoids (polyphenols, mainly curcumin) in turmeric; turmeric is a common cheap substitute or adulterant for saffron (science, chemistry). Real; facts kept general. No live R6_individual item uses spices or pigments (live ones: coffee and cashew, rice and wheat, golden and marsupial moles, steel and concrete, copper and zinc, Guwal and Jalnguy). Band 7 as 4c335aea: the deciding cue (“each spice’s coloration”) sits after the blank in the run, and the joint-possession option C is the close foil; 27 of the 30 run words follow the blank; the first sentence’s “similar golden yellow” pulls toward joint possession, as “trended similarly” does in the model.
band7_moves: individual possession of two mass nouns (section 3, move 9)
deciding cue after the blank: “each spice’s coloration produced by a separate family of compounds” (section 2: deciding word downstream)
joint-possession foil (saffron and turmeric’s) beside the two plural-for-possessive foils, as in 4c335aea
run of 31 words with 29 after the blank

band7.why: Same build as 4c335aea, the only band-7 R6_individual item: the individual-possession cue (“each spice’s coloration produced by a separate family”) sits after the blank, 27 of 30 run words follow it, the joint-possession foil is the close one and the first sentence’s “similar golden yellow” pulls toward it.

fixes: “derive from distinct sources” cut to “are unrelated” (one cue, not three)
“dye textiles, rice, and medicines” to “dye textiles and foods”

items.subtype: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: plural object pronoun (them) for “two faint clouds,” with the Moon and a singular “it” standing between
items.passage: In 1961, Polish astronomer Kazimierz Kordylewski reported two faint clouds of dust orbiting Earth along the same path as the Moon, one traveling ahead of it and one behind. For decades, astronomers struggled to photograph ______, and many doubted that Kordylewski had observed anything at all.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: What astronomers struggled to photograph were the “two faint clouds of dust” that Kordylewski reported. The plural pronoun “them” agrees in number with that plural antecedent.

A.why_wrong: The singular pronoun “it” does not agree with the plural antecedent “clouds”; it would point back to “the Moon,” which astronomers had no trouble photographing.

B.why_wrong: The singular demonstrative “this” does not agree in number with the plural antecedent “clouds.”

D.why_wrong: The singular demonstrative “that” does not agree in number with the plural antecedent “clouds.”

items.notes: Subject: the Kordylewski clouds, dust clouds at the Earth-Moon Lagrange points L4 and L5, reported by Kazimierz Kordylewski in 1961 and long disputed until a Hungarian team imaged one with polarizing filters in 2018 (science, astronomy). Real; facts kept general. Medium as 2.4 and 2.15: a singular rival noun (“the Moon”), already picked up by “it” in the same sentence, sits between the plural antecedent and the blank. Options follow 1.12 (them; this, that, it); no plural or indefinite pronoun is offered, so only one option agrees.

items.subtype: Tense, past perfect: an earlier past before a dated event (By the time Parker received her patent ... for generations)

items.subtype: Finite vs nonfinite: second verb of a compound predicate, split from the first by a dash-enclosed appositive
items.passage: In the early 1950s, Japanese engineer Taiichi Ohno set out to eliminate waste at the Toyota machine shop he managed. Ohno introduced kanban—paper cards that signaled when a workstation needed more parts from the preceding station—and ______ the enormous stockpiles of unused components that had crowded the factory floor.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject “Ohno” has two verbs joined by “and”: he “introduced” kanban, and he did something to the stockpiles. The blank needs a second finite past tense verb parallel with “introduced,” so “reduced” is correct; the dash-enclosed phrase between the two verbs only describes kanban.

A.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: -ing
A.why_wrong: The participle “reducing” cannot serve as the second main verb joined to “introduced” by “and.”

B.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: to + base
B.why_wrong: The infinitive “to reduce” cannot serve as the second main verb joined to “introduced” by “and.”

D.recipe: nonfinite where a finite verb is needed: having + past participle
D.why_wrong: The phrase “having reduced” is nonfinite and cannot serve as the second main verb in the compound predicate.

items.notes: Subject: Taiichi Ohno, who as manager of a Toyota machine shop in the early 1950s introduced kanban cards so that each process drew parts from the one before it only as needed, cutting stocks of parts (social science, business and engineering). Real; facts kept general. Reviewer replacement: the Gunta Stölzl draft was a third Bauhaus woman weaver (Anni Albers live, Otti Berger staged). Medium as 2.1 (band 6): the second verb of a compound predicate split from the first by a dash pair. Canonical option set {finite, -ing, to + base, having + participle}. Each option tested in full: only “reduced” completes the compound predicate.
